To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the effects on the muscle metabolism of beta‐blockers are different from those of other drugs used for the treatment of essential hypertension.
beta blockers do not affect muscle glycogen breakdown during exercise in man, but that the translocation of muscle lactate to the blood is reduced during beta blockade.

1) beta blockade impairs translocation of lactates from muscle to blood, and this is greater when β2‐receptor blockade is added to the β1‐blockade, 2) muscle glycogen breakdown occurs in the presence of beta blockade, and 3) the metabolic effect is not dependent on the type of beta blocker used, but on the type of muscle fibers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of β1‐ and combined β1/β‐2 adrenoceptor blockade on the metabolic responses in skeletal muscle in man.
the hemodynamic and metabolic effects of long‐term β1‐ and beta1/β2 ‐adrenoceptor blockade on muscle tissue during exercise in young hypertensive patients.
the effects of antihypertension therapy on muscle metabolism and the relationship between the metabolic effects and the receptor selectivity of the β‐adrenoceptor blocking drugs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
β‐blockers have no metabolic effect on muscle during antihyertensive treatment.
beta‐blockade, at least at the doses used, does not seem to have a major influence on the metabolic events in muscle during exercise in man.
β1‐adrenergic blockade does not affect muscle glycogen breakdown during exercise, and that β2‐adrenergics do not affect muscle glycogenesis during the recovery period after exercise.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
beta blockade does not impair muscle metabolism during submaximal physical activity in patients with essential hypertension.
beta blockers do not impair muscle metabolism during exercise in man.
beta blockade does not impair the muscle metabolic response to exercise.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of beta‐blockers on muscle metabolism are not as simple as previously thought.
β‐adrenoceptor blockers do not impair muscle metabolism during exercise.

β‐adrenoceptor antagonists do not affect muscle glycogen utilization during exercise, and that the effect of alprenolon is greater than that of atenolol on the lactate translocation from the muscle cell.
